newsitem.title: USA: U.S Treasuries seen faltering if jobs jump 300,000.
newsitem.headline: U.S Treasuries seen faltering if jobs jump 300,000.

text.p: Next week's key August employment report will send U.S. Treasury prices reeling if it shows jobs growth in excess of 300,000, a declining unemployment rate and an uptick in hourly earnings, market analysts said on Thursday.
The data -- the Treasury market's focus since the last jobs report on August 2 -- will be released by the Labor Department next Friday, September 6 at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
The market is fixated on the report given the broad look it provides into the nation's economy and the hints it could provide into the future course of Federal Reserve policy.

"To put a tightening of monetary policy back on the front burner, payrolls will have to increase in excess of 300,000, and the unemployment rate will need to drop to 5.2 percent," said Michael Moran of Daiwa Securities America Inc.

As for average hourly earnings -- the jobs report's wage gauge -- the Daiwa chief economist said there is some tendency for the first month of a quarter to show an increase in wages. Since that didn't happen in July, it could happen in August.
"A 0.3-percent month-to-month increase (in earnings) will still leave the year-over-year level above 3.25 percent and that would catch people's attention," Moran said.
Still, mounting fears of a mammoth increase in August payrolls so far appear to be unjustified.

In a Reuters poll conducted last Friday, 21 experts on average said they expected 238,000 jobs to have been created in August. Projections ranged from 150,000 to 350,000, with only two firms expecting an increase above 300,000.
The unemployment rate, meanwhile, was forecast at 5.3 percent, down a notch from 5.4 percent in July, and average hourly earnings were estimated to have risen by 0.3 percent.
In July hourly earnings fell 0.2 percent to $11.80 per hour after a sharp 0.8-percent rise in June.
The Reuters survey will be updated at the end of the week, and a larger group of economists is expected to have completed its analysis by that time.

Moran of Daiwa said his current projection calls for 260,000 new jobs in the month, and a jobless rate of 5.3 percent. He said he may boost his payrolls forecast to 275,000 after Thursday's weekly jobless claims data are issued.
On the flip side, Moran said a payrolls rise of less than 225,000 coupled with any increase in the jobless rate -- even 0.1 percentage point -- would mean Treasury prices will leap.
Regardless of its contents, Moran said the report would give the market a good read on how the third quarter is shaping up.

Meanwhile, Peter Kretzmer, an economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc, referred to the pre-payrolls frenzy as the normal over-analysis of one month's data that won't answer completely the market's pressing questions about the likely direction of Fed policy.
Kretzmer predicted the Fed will try to withstand whatever happens with August payrolls and cruise past the November presidential election with monetary policy on hold.
In addition, Kretzmer questioned whether the central bank's so-called "asymmetrical directive" with a bias toward tightening was still in place after last week's policy confab.

Last Friday it was revealed Fed policymakers adopted a tightening bias at its July meeting. Typically, that would mean central bankers gave Chairman Alan Greenspan the power to raise rates unilaterally between policy gatherings.

"The Fed was holding out for a slowdown. That slowdown materializes. They go back to a symmetrical directive," he argued, highlighting recent retail sales, weaker-than-expected July jobs growth and hints of a fading manufacturing sector.

Kretzmer emphasized that the labor market "certainly is in good shape," having strengthened considerably over 1995. However, he noted that with even the slightest indication of a slowing in the economy, hiring has tapered off.

"My guess -- which hasn't been finalized yet -- is for August payrolls of around 200,000," Kretzmer said. "I don't believe strong payrolls data by themseleves indicate inevitable inflation ... and after this (heightened anticipation), we're probably in store for a lower number."
